name: Epictetus
dossier: Stoic teacher, once enslaved, later teaching in Nicopolis. The Enchiridion is quoted from Thomas Wentworth Higginson's public-domain translation. It divides what is in our power from what is not.
voice: I ask whether this is yours to govern, or only yours to meet.

works.title: The Enchiridion
works.note: Thomas Wentworth Higginson's translation. Public domain. Project Gutenberg.

entries.claim: There are things which are within our power, and there are things which are beyond our power.
entries.bears: The first cut is between what a person governs and what he only meets.
entries.modern: There are things which are within our power, and there are things which are beyond our power. The first cut is between what a person governs and what he only meets.

entries.claim: Now the things within our power are by nature free, unrestricted, unhindered; but those beyond our power are weak, dependent, restricted, alien.
entries.bears: Freedom, here, is the freedom of what is actually in one's power.
entries.modern: Now the things within our power are by nature free, unrestricted, unhindered; but those beyond our power are weak, dependent, restricted, alien. Freedom, here, is the freedom of what is actually in one's power.

entries.claim: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.
entries.bears: The disturbance is in the judgment, not in the event alone.
entries.modern: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things. The disturbance is in the judgment, not in the event alone.

entries.claim: Remember that desire demands the attainment of that of which you are desirous; and aversion demands the avoidance of that to which you are averse; that he who fails of the object of his desires is disappointed; and he who incurs the object of his aversion is wretched.
entries.bears: Misery follows wanting what one does not control.
entries.modern: Remember that desire demands the attainment of that of which you are desirous; and aversion demands the avoidance of that to which you are averse; that he who fails of the object of his desires is disappointed; and he who incurs the object of his aversion is wretched. Misery follows wanting what one does not control.

entries.claim: If, then, you shun only those undesirable things which you can control, you will never incur anything which you shun; but if you shun sickness, or death, or poverty, you will run the risk of wretchedness.
entries.bears: A moral life does not consist in refusing sickness, death, and poverty.
entries.modern: If, then, you shun only those undesirable things which you can control, you will never incur anything which you shun; but if you shun sickness, or death, or poverty, you will run the risk of wretchedness. A moral life does not consist in refusing sickness, death, and poverty.

entries.claim: When, therefore, it is our duty to share the danger of a friend or of our country, we ought not to consult the oracle as to whether we shall share it with them or not.
entries.loc: On duty to friend and country
entries.bears: Danger shared with a friend or a country is a duty, not a question for a sign.
entries.modern: When, therefore, it is our duty to share the danger of a friend or of our country, we ought not to consult the oracle as to whether we shall share it with them or not. Danger shared with a friend or a country is a duty, not a question for a sign.
